newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Puerto Rico lawmakers okay sale of phone company.
newsitem.headline: Puerto Rico lawmakers okay sale of phone company.

text.p: Puerto Rico was preparing Wednesday to open negotiations for the sale of the government-owned telephone company, one of the largest privatisations in Latin America in recent years.
Lawmakers in this Caribbean U.S. commonwealth gave final approval Tuesday to the legislation that paved the way for sale of the Puerto Rico Telephone Co. (PRTC)
The bill was to be sent to Gov. Pedro Rossello, who was expected to sign it immediately to open bidding on the PRTC, one of Puerto Rico's most profitable public corporations.
Earnings have increased from $800 million in 1991 to $1.1 billion in 1997.

But PRTC lost its monopoly on local service following the passage of the 1996 Federal Telecommunications Reform Act and government officials have expressed concern about it competing with the likes of MCI Communications Corp. and AT&T Corp..
The sale faced stiff opposition from the Telephone Workers United Front, an umbrella group of two unions that represent the PRTC's 6,200 unionized employees.
Annie Cruz, president of the Brotherhood of Independent Telephone Workers, has called the sale the "rip-off of the century" and accused Rossello of "selling the national patrimony."

Cruz said her union and others were contemplating a massive one-day strike aimed at shutting down the island. Union telephone workers staged a one-day work stoppage on July 11, disabling the company's 411 and 811 information services.
"We're going to paralyse this island completely," Cruz said. No date had been set for the general strike.
Companies frequently mentioned as expressing interest in the phone company are Telefonica de Espana, Bell Atlantic-NYNEX, and AT&T.

The Puerto Rico telephone market is still expanding, according to industry figures. About 74 percent of island residents have telephone service, compared with 90 percent penetration in the United States as a whole.

The government, under a different administration, tried to sell PRTC in 1990 for about $3 billion, including assumption of its $1 billion debt. But the sale fell through because of burdensome amendments imposed by legislators that made the deal less attractive to investors.
Among the final bidders at that time were Bell South and GTE Corp..

Lawmakers attached several amendments this year, one that would require the buyer to pay local taxes and guarantee the jobs of about 2,000 non-union managerial employees for one year after the sale is approved by the Federal Communications Commission.

The proposed work stoppage could include, in addition to telephone workers, union members of state-owned water and power authorities and employees in the trucking and shipping sectors among others, Cruz said. Up to 60 unions were expected to participate.
"Forget about doing any business in Puerto Rico on that day," Cruz said. "We're going to shut it down."
